title: Restitution as an independent basis of liability
shortTitle: Restitution as an independent basis of liability
summary: Unjust enrichment concerns a benefit that a defendant has received at another person’s expense and that the law regards as unjust to retain without payment or return.
notes:
This basis of liability can arise without an enforceable promise. The casebook distinguishes mistaken benefits and justified emergency interventions from unrequested services voluntarily imposed on a recipient. A benefit alone is therefore insufficient. Ask who received what, why the claimant supplied it, and why retention would be unjust. Restitution also appears later as a remedy following breach, where an existing agreement and its termination affect the analysis.

The introduction gives mistaken payments, mistakenly performed services, and improvements to another’s property as examples. It distinguishes a mistaken transfer from an unrequested benefit voluntarily imposed by an officious intermeddler. When bargaining is feasible, the text explains why a person cannot ordinarily force someone else to pay for an unsolicited service. Emergency intervention can present a different question. The following Cotnam opinion begins on the last assigned page, so its full reasoning is not available within the assignment.
